title: August and the Horizon
premise: Marguerite Okonkwo has kept Earth's last seed vault running alone for seven years, invisible among the cargo haulers threading contested orbits. When a manifest lists a passenger aboard a ship that was decommissioned before she ever arrived, she uncovers a hidden cryobay holding two thousand sleepers—half chosen by the old government, half by the mutineers who seized the vault's reactor. As the reactor's failsafe countdown forces her to wake only one group, Marguerite must choose between the truth of who built the lists and the loyalty she owes the found family of scavengers who kept her alive. In the end she refuses the binary, sacrificing the vault's seed stores as reactor coolant to buy time to wake both halves, and departs with her crew to seed a new world from what remains.
about_author: Emrys Delacroix is the pen name of a former orbital logistics analyst who spent a decade writing technical manuals for deep-space storage facilities. They now write science fiction about the quiet people who keep humanity's machinery running after everyone else has gone.

chapters.title: The Weight of Empty Bays
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A routine supply run through contested orbits establishes her solitary life tending the seed vault and her fragile bond with the scavenger crew of the Kestrel. The emotional beat is weary contentment—she has made peace with being forgotten, and the chapter makes that peace feel earned.

chapters.title: A Name That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Auditing manifests during a reactor maintenance cycle, she finds a passenger listed on the Meridian, a ship decommissioned years before her arrival. The name matches no crew record. The beat is a cold prickle of wrongness that unravels her carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Reactor Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating between Marguerite and Jun, the Kestrel's engineer. Following power draws that don't match the logs, they find a sealed cryobay behind the reactor shielding: two thousand sleepers in two segregated blocks, each block with its own authorization list. The beat is awe curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Two Lists
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Decoding the lists reveals one compiled by the pre-collapse government, one by the mutineers who seized the vault—and her own predecessor's signature on both. A countdown begins when the bay's seal breaks: ninety days before the reactor purges everything. The beat is guilt: her seven years of silence fed this secret.

chapters.title: The Kestrel Decides
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV across the scavenger crew. Some want to sell the discovery to the orbit factions; others want to wake their own dead; the youngest, Tovi, argues for everyone. Loyalty fractures along the fault line of profit versus principle. The beat is found family under its first real strain.

chapters.title: Ghost Signal
chapters.summary: Jun's POV. Someone else has noticed the power anomaly—a faction warship begins shadowing the vault, broadcasting demands using the predecessor's voiceprint. Marguerite realizes the mutineers' AI has been awake all along, watching her. The beat is paranoia closing in like a hand around the throat.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The faction docks by force; in the confrontation, the truth surfaces—the predecessor chose neither list, but rigged the bay so waking either half would doom the other, ensuring mutual destruction out of spite. The countdown accelerates. The beat is betrayal, and Marguerite's refusal to inherit that spite.

chapters.title: Coolant
chapters.summary: Jun and Tovi's POV. The only way to slow the purge is to vent the seed vault's own atmosphere reserves and sacrifice irreplaceable seed stock as thermal mass. The crew votes—unanimously, this time—to spend the past to save the future. The beat is grief transformed into resolve.

chapters.title: Both Doors Open
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, climax. With the faction boarding and the reactor at critical margin, she overrides both lists simultaneously, waking all two thousand in staggered waves while the Kestrel runs interference. She nearly dies sealing the final breach. The beat is the choice itself: belonging means refusing to let anyone be disposable.

chapters.title: August and the Horizon
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, resolution. Weeks later, the woken sleepers and the scavenger crew rebuild together aboard a refitted station, planting the salvaged seeds in hydroponic bays. Marguerite, once invisible, is asked to speak first at the founding assembly. The beat is quiet arrival: she finally belongs somewhere she helped choose.
